state.misconception_label: Does not understand that 2n represents an even number

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Which of these shows part of the proof that the sum of two odd numbers is even? I got \( \begin{array}{l}2 n+(2 m+1) \\ =2(n+m)+1\end{array} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of the variables n and m as representing two friends counting marbles. If one friend has 2 marbles and the other has 2 marbles plus one more, together they have an even number of marbles. Can you see how this relates to the equation you wrote out?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, so you're saying 2n is like 2 marbles, and 2m+1 is like 2 marbles plus one more? But then when I add them together I got 2(n+m)+1, which still has the +1 at the end... doesn't that mean it's odd, not even? I'm confused about why that would prove the sum is even.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine that n and m are two teams playing a game. If one team has 2 players, and the other team has 2 players plus one more, when they join forces, they will have an even number of players on the field. So, when you add 2n and 2m+1 together, you end up with 2(n+m)+1, which still gives you an even total number of players. Can you see how this example helps to show that the sum of two odd numbers is even?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Wait, but I'm still confused... if we end up with 2(n+m)+1, that has a +1 at the end, so shouldn't that make it odd? Like, 2 times something plus 1 is always odd, right? I don't see how that proves it's even...

score.justification_pass1: The teacher repeatedly provides analogies that reinforce incorrect mathematics (claiming 2(n+m)+1 is even), fails to address the student's actual misconception about representing odd numbers as 2n+1 and 2m+1, and the student ends more confused than at the start.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher consistently uses concrete real-world analogies (marbles, teams/players), these analogies are mathematically incorrect and fail to ground the abstract concept properly, as they incorrectly suggest that 2(n+m)+1 represents an even number when it actually represents an odd number.
